speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: This is to cover the expenses of the following officials:	Homestead inspectors, inspectors of land agencies, inspectors of branches, Dominion lands and Crown timber agencies and sub-land-agencies, and to provide for any additional help that may be required during the year, or for any increases in salaries.
There is no increase?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: No.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I would like to ask the Minister of the Interior if he
intends to spend all of this money, or if he wants to be economical and retrench somewhat. We have just heard the statement of the hon. Minister of Finance (Sir Thomas White) that the Government will not expend the whole of their Estimates. Does that apply to the Department of the Interior? It is a very wrong practice to make the Estimates larger than the intended expenditure. The Estimates which have been brought down provide for an expenditure on consolidated fund account of $153,958,730.58. In the Budget speech the Minister of Finance stated that he did not contemplate expending $158,000,000. but only $125,000,000, if I understood him aright. Therefore, to provide in the Estimates for $33,000,000 more than you intend to expend, is a very wrong practice. I do not want to enter into a discussion with the Minister of the Interior on that point; I will discuss it with the Minister of Finance. Does my hon. friend intend to expend the whole of the amount that he is asking for, or is he going to economize.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: I might explain to my right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition, that this is to provide for the salaries of 463 officials. Of these there are some 55 who have enlisted and whose places we have not as yet been filled.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: And which vou will not fill?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: ' Not unless it is absolutely essential.
Are you paying their salaries?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Those who enlisted prior to the 1st of November, 1915, are drawing their civil pay and their military pay; but those who enlisted after that date receive only their military pay and the difference between that and their civil pay.
Why not put them all on the same basis? .

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
We are governed by an Order in Council which applies to the whole service. On account of the pretty heavy drain on the war fund to pay these salaries and the salaries of substitutes, we thought it wise to impose some safeguard, and in consequence the Order in Council was passed that those who enlisted after the 1st of November, 1915, should receive, not their civil pay and their military pay, but merely their military pay and the difference between that and their civil pay.

818 '

I understand that the Order in Council passed on the 1st of November applies to all departments. Suppose a young man in one of the departments wishes to qualify as a commissioned officer, either a captain or a lieutenant; is he allowed any portion of his salary while he is attending one of the training schools, say in Quebec or Halifax? Is he obliged to pay his own expenses while at the school?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: We have allowed leave of absence with pay to those who have left for the training school, as some of them have. Of course, if they go to the school after they enlist, they receive their military pay while there.
Is that done under a general Order in Council, ot is it a matter of favoritism by the head of the department?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: So far as leave of absence is concerned, I do not think there is any general Order in Council. A few men in my department have asked me for leave of absence to attend one of these training schools, and I have always granted it.
Where leave of absence is granted, then, the men receive pay during their absence under a general Order in Council?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Yes, under the general Order in Council.

The reason I bring this up is that I know of a young man in the employ of the Government who wished to attend one of these training schools. The information he has been given is that he will have to forfeit his pay during the time he is at the training school. I am therefore very glad to hear the minister say that there is a general Order in Council, applying to all departments, that these young men shall receive pay while at the training school. This is a very important matter, for this reason. These young men cannot very well afford to pay their own expenses and lose their pay. All of them have to have uniforms before they can attend the school, and I believe they are obliged to buy their uniforms themselves. If that is the case, it strikes me as very unfair, and I think it will prevent many thoroughly good young men who would make splendid officers from attending the school. A man, for instance, earning two or three dollars a day, would have to spend two or three months' wages in buying his

uniform. This is a very important matter, and I am therefore glad to hear the minister say that the men in the departments are allowed their pay while at the training school.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Either the hon. gentleman misunderstood me or I misunderstood him. I did not wish to give the impression that there is a general Order in Council allowing pay to any person in the department while he is qualifying at one of the training schools. There is no general Order in Council to that effect. The Order in Council of November 1 simply provides that those who enlist on and after the 1st of November shall receive only their military pay and the difference between that and their civil pay. Those who enlisted previous to that date draw both their civil pay and their military pay. Prior to the 1st of November we did not make this distinction.

Perhaps the minister misunderstood my question, or he may have received different information since he gave his answer. But in answer to my question he said that to the men in his department he had granted leave of absence to attend a training school, and that their pay had been allowed to go on while they were at the school. Does the minister wish to withdraw that statement?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: I can only answer for my own department. There is no general Order in Council covering such a case. I have in all cases allowed young men in my department who wanted to attend the training school three weeks' holidays, and three weeks additional leave of absence with pay. The course takes about six weeks, I think.

They get paid during the whole six weeks?
.Mr. ROCHE: Yes.
If this is simply a matter of favouritism by the head of the department, it is entirely wrong.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: I have allowed leave of absence in every case.

But other ministers have not. There should he a general Order in Council providing for the same practice in every department. It is entirely unjust that while employees of the Department of the Interior are granted three weeks' holidays, and a further three weeks' leave with pay, to attend a training school, em-

ployees of other departments of the Government are denied the same right. There should be one rule, and only one rule, applying to all departments. It is a very great hardship that any of these young men should be deprived of their pay during the period they are qualifying at the training school, and that they should have to pay for their own uniforms. This is a state of affairs which prevents the country from having [DOT] the benefit of the services of hundreds of young, men who, while they have not much of this world's goods, would make just as valuable officers as the sons of wealthy parents, and in many cases better.
Did I understand the minister to say that all those in his department who enlisted previous to the 1st oi November, 1915, enjoy their civil salaries in addition to their military pay?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Yes.

A man drawing three or four thousand dollars a year from this Government might enlist prior to the 1st of November, and be appointed to a military position paying two or three thousand dollars a year. Would that man get both salaries?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: I do not think there has been a case of that nature in my department, and I think there would be very few such cases in any of the departments. But that is the principle.

On what grounds does
the Government justify paying a man who enlists on. the last day of October both his civil and military pay, and a man who enlists on the 1st of November only his military pay, and the difference between that and his civil pay? If that practice is followed there will be no harmony in the departments of the Government nor in the trenches. I am not speaking particularly against either system, although I think the latter system is the best; but I say that all the men should be treated alike: put them all under one system or under the other. I do not think the present system is fair. A man drawing a large salary from this Government may be appointed to a position in the service overseas, carrying with it a laTge salary. That position may take the man into the trenches, or he may be miles away from the trenches, and in no more danger than in a civil position in the city of Ottawa. Why should such a man be allowed to
52i
draw two big salaries just because he happened to enlist prior to the 1st of November? Why distinguish between those who enlist before the 1st of November and those who enlist after? If it is wrong to pay a man both his military pay and his civil pay, why does the Government continue to do it? As the Minister of Finance pointed out this afternoon, we do not know in what position we are in this war; we may be only at the beginning of it. We must, therefore, conserve our resources and we ' must practise economy. If the Government wants the people of Canada to economize, the Government should set the example; but it is not showing that example of economy that we would like to see, especially in some cases that I have in mind, though not in the department of my hon. friend. Some explanation ought certainly to be given as to why a distinction is made between men joining before the first of November and men joining after that date.

I wish to ask the hon. gentleman a question in regard to promotion after enlistment. Take, for instance, an official in the Post Office Department, who is entitled to promotion from one grade to another after a certain examination. If such an official has enlisted, is he still entitled to that promotion?
I must say that I find the distinction quite invidious between soldiers or officers who enlisted before the first of November last and those who enlisted after that date. It might happen that certain men were not of age or were not ready to enlist before the first of November last, and because they enlisted on the first or second of November last, there would be an invidious distinction made as to the amount of money they would draw from the department. Now, it seems to me that this war is being waged for the principle of equal rights. Is it fair, then, among men of the same national family who are fighting in the trenches one should be able to say to another: I enlisted on the 30th of October, being an official of this or that department, and I receive my full monthly salary, whilst you, my comrade, because you were not of age or had not at that time passed the medical examination enlisted on the first or on the second of November, and receive less than I do. This is not fair, and the Government should apply to all the policy which it has adopted by the terms of the Order in

Council of the first of November last. The same treatment should be meted out to every member of the Canadian expeditionary force. They are all fighting the same enemy; let them fight on the same terms and with equal rights.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: In regard to the first point raised by my hon. friend that promotions have been refused to wiose

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: I understand that the Civil Service Commission has refused to sanction such promotions.

I have in my mind
the Post Office Department, because that is the department over which I formerly presided. Perhaps my hon. friend the Postmaster General (Mr. Casgrain) could explain this matter to me. There are various grades in the outside service. , A man may enter the service at a salary of say $600, and after twelve months or twenty-four months he is entitled to promotion, provided he passes a certain examination. Will that officer, being in the expeditionary force, be entitled to that promotion which he would have received had he been on duty in Canada?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
If he has to
pass an examination, obviously he cannot lie promoted.
He cannot pass it, because he is on service overseas.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The Civil Service Act would control that.

Why was the change
made on the first of November? No reason has yet been given.
Mr.' ROCHE: I have explained the reason. Substitutes for civfl servants who have gone to the front have to be paid out of the war appropriation, and we felt that there was too big a drain on it. That was one reason that led us to make the change. Hon. members who have spoken seem to think that the present system is the proper one, that is, only to pay these men the deference between their military and their civil pay, but they wish to go further and reduce the pay of those who enlisted prior to the first of November. I do not agree
| M r. I.emkrUX. ]
with that proposition, because it would be a breach of contract. All those men enlisted on certain conditions, and, as they did so enlist and went overseas, to reduce their pay would not be doing justice to them; but we are not doing any injustice to those who have enlisted since the first of November, because they know in advance what pay they are going to receive.

I have in mind an appointment made by the Minister of the Interior in October, 1914, to a position commanding a salary of $1,800, a year. There was no attempt made to justify the appointment on the ground that it was necessary; in fact, the duties assigned to the young 5 p.m. man who was appointed had been discharged by another official, who had a smaller salary. About the first of August, 1915, this young man enlisted in one of the regiments which were being recruited at Halifax. He has undergone some training and up to the present time he is in Halifax still enjoying his salary of $1,800 a year, as well as the allowance made to him by the Militia Department in his rank of lieutenant. I do not know what the salary of a lieutenant is, but I presume it is a respectable sum.
$125 a month.

Then he is in receipt of $275 a month, if you take into account his civil and his military pay. When the minister's Estimates were up last year, I pointed out to him that the appointment of this man was entirely unjustifiable, because the other official had never complained tfcat the duties were too arduous, nor that his territory .was too large for him to cover. The appointment was, I say, for the purpose of giving this young man a position, and the country was doing very well when it provided him with a salary of $1,800 a year. Now, by reason of the policy adopted by the Department of the Interior prior to the first of November last, this man enjoys the additional salary which comes to him as a lieutenant. The duties of the position to which he was appointed in the Department of the Interior are being discharged by the gentleman who has discharged them during the last seven or eight years. I have no fault to find with the treatment that has been accorded to this young man in Halifax, but I do think there is no logical reason why those men who enlisted since November 1, should not have the same privilege as to salary as those who enlisted previous to that date. I

am informed that employes of other departments who volunteered for service previous to November 1, were told that they would not receive their salaries as civil servants if they joined the forces. I am not in a position to vouch for the accuracy of this, but it has been a matter of complaint in the province of Nova Scotia that the same rule has not been made applicable to the employees of all departments of Government.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: To what regiment is this gentleman attached?

I am not in a position to
say.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: What position did he hold in the department?

He was Superintendent of
Indian Agencies in the Maritime provinces.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: That does not come under the Department of the Interior.

My hon. friend said a
moment ago that he thought it would be a breach of contract if those who enlisted prior to November 1, 1914, did not continue to receive their double salaries. That is to say, in effect, that that class of men joined the colours simply because they wanted to get the double salary.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Not necessarily.

It practically amounts
to that. If these men have any complaint, it is that they would not have joined had they known that they were not to receive their salaries as civil servants. If, as the Minister of Finance said to-day, we desire to do our part to carry the war through successfully, we must economize. The Minister of the Interior is a level-headed, reasonable man; does he think it is reasonable that a political position should be created for the gentleman referred to by the hon.memberfor Richmond (Mr. Kyte), when there was no more need for his services than there is for a fifth wheel to a wagon? He has not gone overseas; a great many men who enlisted in the early part of the war are shirking their duties, and have absolutely no intention of going to the war. I have in mind the case of a man who was drawing a salary of $80 a month. He joined the army, and his wife is now getting his salary, $80 a month, besides separation allowance, part of her husband's pay as a soldier, and, I think, an allowance from the Patriotic Fund. So that she has plenty of money to spend, and is making no attempt to save it. That is the kind of economy
that my hon. friend recommends; it is not the economy referred to in the splendid speech of the Minister of Finance this afternoon. I agree with the Minister of Finance that in order to bring the war to a successful issue we must expand our production, develop our resources, and practise economy, and what kind of example is this department giving us? I consider the case brought forward by the hon. member for Richmond to be a strong indictment against this Government, and I think it would be well if the Minister of Interior should get from the Minister of Militia a statement of the amount being paid to this official, and the nature of the duties which are still occupying his attention in Halifax, notwithstanding the fact that he enlisted in the early days of the war. There may be a good reason for his not going overseas, but I do know of many cases where men who joined early in the war are still strutting round in their frills and feathers without the slightest intention of going to the front.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I cannot concur in the observation of my hon. friend that a considerable number of persons who have enlisted desire to avoid over-seap service. My experience teaches me that the young men of Canada who have enlisted have been'eminently desirous
The great majority, certainly.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: In almost every individual instance they have desired to go to the front.
No.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: My hon. friend takes issue with me on that. I am speaking only of my own experience; perhaps he may have had a different experience. As to the young man to whom my hon. friend from Richmond has alluded, if he will send me his name I certainly will have that matter looked into, because I cannot understand why any young man who enlisted for everseas service more than a year ago-
I said he enlisted in August of 1915. He was appointed to his present position in October, 1914.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I thought he had been amusing himself for more than a year.

I .misunderstood what
the hon. member said. I thought he had enlisted in August, 1914, instead of August, 1915.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Of course, we
know that some regiments have been kept in Canada for rather prolonged periods of training. That has not always been due to any desire or action of the Canadian Government; it has been due very often to the inability of the British authorities either to provide transport or to furnish suitable accommodation for the men on the other side. An Order in Council was passed in the early weeks of the war providing that persons in the Civil Service of Canada who enlisted for overseas service would be paid their salaries during the time they were so serving their country at the front. At that time it was not anticipated that the war would last so long, and we had before us at that time the example of municipal corporations and railway and other corporations throughout Canada that were proposing to do exactly the same thing. The idea was impressed on the Government that the country could hardly afford to be less generous with regard to men who were prepared to make the supreme sacrifice than private corporations throughout the country. As the war went on and a greater number of forces had to be recruited, it became evident to the Government that some question might arise as to the* continued efficiency of the public service if men were allowed to go on these terms. Moreover, we could not let them go without any consideration of the question whether their services would be more valuable to the country and the Empire at the front or in the performance of the duties they had hitherto discharged. After a good deal of consideration it was proposed that the Order in Council which has been laid on the Table should be passed. I am not quite clear as to the views of hon. gentlemen opposite; perhaps they may not all have the same view. It has been suggested by some of them that we should immediately pass an Order in Council amending the Order in Council of 1914 and providing that these men should no longer be paid the salaries to which they were entitled under that order. There are other hon. gentlemen who seem to take the ground that the order of November last should not have been passed and that we should continue to pay all civil servants who go to the front the full amount of their salaries in addition to their pay and their allowance as soldiers. We did not adopt either of these courses, but provided that civil servants hereafter going to the front should go on certain conditions which they well under-
stood before enlisting. They know perfectly well when they enlist the terms on which the Government think civil servants should be permitted to give up their duties in Canada and go to the front to serve in a military capacity. Of course, when we adopted a policy of that kind some date had to be fixed and we fixed, I think, the 1st of November last. Every civil servant who has enlisted on or since that date has enlisted under terms and oonditions which were perfectly well known to him at the time. In addition to that, we had to consider, when a man desired to go to the front, whether or not the duties which he had been performing in the department could be discharged without the engagement of some other person to take his place, to whom an additional salary would have to be paid. The considerations which have been alluded to by the Minister of the Interior were before us in that regard. So we thought that, under the circumstances, the best solution of the matter was along the lines whicn the Government have pursued. ' But if my hon. friends opposite have any definite concrete suggestions as to some other solution which in their judgment is better, we should be very glad to have their suggestions. We made the Order in Council in the first instance in the expectation that the war would not last nearly so long, and we made it having regard to similar proposals which had been made by municipal and other corporations in the country. When the war did last for such a very considerable period, in view of the increased additional strain put on the public service by reason of the duration of dhe war and of the greatly increased number of men we are sending, we came to the conclusion that some change should be made, and it was made along that line.

One can readily understand the situation in which the Government found themselves at the beginning of the war. At that time no person, in Canada at least, anticipated that the war would be either so serious ot so long drawn out. Municipalities and other institutions were granting pay or part pay to those in their service who enlisted, and the. Government did likewise. But the conditions have so changed now that it is a serious matter just to decide what ought to be done. This condition confronts one now in discussing the question of enlisting with the ordinary young man: the man in the Civil Service, under the first regulation, is getting in some

instances double pay, and is twice as well off from a financial standpoint as he was before he enlisted. Looking at it only from that viewpoint, he has made no sacrifice; he has made an improvement. Under the second Order in Council the man who is sufficiently fortunate to be in the Civil Service is not making any financial sacrifice; he is in the same position financially as he would have been had he not enlisted. But when you come to the average young man in the country, he is making the supreme sacrifice, he is giving up his employment, giving up perhaps the futnre prospect of it when he comes back, and is taking instead the smaill amount given to him as a private. Financially he is really giving up his entire future. It is difficult to have the best feeling prevailing when you find two men side by side, one better off financially than he was before enlisting, and the other having made the great sacrifice of giving up his salary and any chance of promotion if he was employed by some person or some company. On the other hand, we have thousands of young men in Canada who are locking the doors of their business establishments, so far as they are concerned, young prac-tioners who have just started in the practice of their profession, who are just getting, as it were, on their feet. They are giving up their prospects, locking the door, settling their little businesses, and going overseas for, perhaps, twenty per cent, or twenty-five per cent of what they had hoped to make. It is difficult to convince them of the reasonableness of the man side by side with them being so much better off financially and making no sacrifice in that respect, while they sacrifice everything. It is a difficult situation, and one requiring serious consideration. I think the step the Government have taken towards reducing the amount so that those in the service are not getting any more pay than before they enlisted was a reasonable one, and if the war is to continue perhaps another step will have to be made, so that every man in Canada will be on an equal footing as to the sacrifice he is required to make for the country.

I do not wish to discuss the concrete cases mentioned by my hon. friend from Assiniboia (Mr. Turriff) and my hon. friend from Richmond (Mr. Kyte), but I do feel disposed to say that, the Government having come to an understanding with certain young men prior to their enlistment at the outbreak of the war, it would not, in my opinion, be an honourable course for the Government to go back on that understanding. We believe there should be honour between nations, and we also believe that there should be honour between governments and individuals with whom they deal.

With respect to the men who have actually gone to the front, there is considerable justification for the course taken by the Government; but in cases where the young men have not gone to the front, and are not suffering any more physical or personal discomforts than their neighbours who have not enlisted, I think the minister- should suspend payment of the civil salary until they have actually gone to the front, and not put them in a position to draw double salary while their services to the country are not manifest to the onlooker. I said a moment ago that I had moved in the House for a return of all the employees of the Government who have enlisted since the outbreak of the war, and who are enjoying both civil and military salaries. I would like to ask the minister if he would be good enough to bring down a list of the employees in the Department of the Interior before his Estimates are again under * consideration.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: If my hon. friend means a list of all the officials in the Department of the Interior who have enlisted, and of the salaries they are getting, that list has already been brought down. I handed it to the ex-Minister of the Interior the other day. I think that all the employees in the Department of the Ulterior who enlisted have gone to the front, except in two instances, and in these cases the men are specially required for organization purposes by the Militia Department. The hon. member has not pointed out any instance [DOT] .of an employee of the Interior Department getting double pay who has refused to go to the front.
I did not insinuate that any man had refused to go to the front; I simply referred to oases of young men who had not gone to the front, and who nevertheless were enjoying double salaries.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
No doubt the reason they have not gone is that the regiment has not been moved to the front; but we should not dock a young man of his salary because the Government have not seen fit so far to send his regiment overseas. In that respect the Government are guided by the

British War Office. I think it would be distinctly unfair to dock a young man, who comes within the provision of the original Order in Council, of his civil pay simply because his regiment has not been ordered to the front.

I have no fault to find with the men who are drawing double salary, but I think the Government were guilty of a mistake in making an arrangement which applied only to those who enlisted previous to the first of November, and which they could not carry out in respect to those who enlisted subsequent to the first of November. I think the whole difficulty lies in the circumstance that the Gov ernment had not a well-thought out plan that could be made applicable to all the employees in the different services who have enlisted.

It is true, as the Prime Minister has pointed out, that many companies and municipalities agreed at the commencement of the war to pay salaries to , their employees if they enlisted and went to the front. I should like to cite the case of one large corporation, perhaps the largest railway corporation in Canada, the Canadian Pacific Railway Company. The arrangement they made with their employees who enlisted, was that they received no pay so long as they remained in Canada, but when they went overseas they or their families received it for six months, and then it stopped. That was a fair business arrangement, and an inducement to the men to enlist.

I have looked over the list
brought down by the minister, and I find that it refers only to employees in the inside service. I would like to get a return giving the names of the employees in the outside service who have enlisted.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: There is a return to that effect, and it will be laid on the Table tomorrow.

The right hon. the Prime Minister pointed out that at the time the first and second contingents were sent overseas it was expected that the war would be short, and a certain arrangement was made with the men who enlisted in those contingents. It seems to me that it would not be unreasonable to look upon that arrangement as a limited one. These men joined in the fall of 1914, and many of us, and I imagine the members of the Government themselves, thought that by November of 1915 	j
the war would be practically over. These men enjoyed double salary up to that date, so it does not seem to me that it would be a hardship to say that on the first of November, 1915, they should come under the new *rule. Let me point out to the Prime Minister just how it works out. Take the case of a young man who was earning say $80 a month in his own business or in the eipploy of a merchant or insurance company that did not give any pay at all to the employees who went to the front. That young man loses his $80 a month, and at the rate of $1.10 per day he takes $33 a month from the Government. Out of a sense of duty to his country and to the Empire he makes that sacrifice. Then take the case of a young man who happened to have the good fortune to work for the Government, and who enlisted subsequent to the first of November. He gets say $80 a month. Right beside them is a man who was in the Civil Service and earning say $80 a month, but who joined prior to the first of November last; he draws $80 plus $33 per month. 'There you have three young men, one getting $33 a month, another $80 a month and a third $113 a month. I leave it to this House and to the Prime Minister to say whether that is a satisfactory state of affairs.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
There are no
doubt, anomalies, but my hon. friend will doubtless remember that in respect to the employees of municipalities and great corporations who have gone to the front under arrangements that have been already alluded to, precisely the same condition exists. Any man who was employed by one of those corporations or municipalities, and who has gone into the trenches, naturally has a very much larger income than the man alongside of him who did not happen to be an employee of one of those corporations or municipalities; so that the anomaly could not be removed even if .the Government should take the course, which my hon. friend seems to suggest, of giving them no portion of their salary. The anomaly would still continue in respect to those members of the Canadian Expeditionary Forces who were employed by those corporations and municipalities. You cannot get away from certain anomalies in any case, because our own men "at the front enjoy a pay that is very considerably larger than the pay of the British soldier fighting in the trenches alongside of him. I am not quite sure what the pay of the British soldier is; I think' it is

about a shilling a day; and the pay of the French soldier, at the commencement of the war, if I remember correctly, was two cents a day.

It has been increased to
five cents a day.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I think it was
originally two cents a day. But, as a matter of fact, in regard to these men who have gone from Canada, whether they are employees of the Government or of any municipality or of any corporation, I for one decline to believe that the question of the remuneration which they were to receive had much to do with it. I believe these men went from a sense of duty. Undoubtedly there are some anomalies which we have endeavoured to correct along the lines laid down by my hon. friend from Wright (Mr. Devlin), who expressed views in regard to our undertaking any change in the arrangements made which were practically those I had expressed to the House before. I am afraid that we could not cure all the anomalies, even if the Government should take the action which my hon. friend thought we should have taken in the first instance. I do not believe that any one in Canada or in the Empire, outside possibly of a few military experts, thought, in the opening months of the war, that it would last for anything like the [DOT] period during which it is likely to continue; so that arrangements were made having regard to a probable duration much shorter than the period which it has proved necessary to provide for.

I think the Government
should give notice in the future of any change which they intend making. Any bargain you have made should be lived up to. If a man has gone under certain conditions the Government cannot break the engagement. If we are going to have 250,000 mqre men, and it is doubtful that we can raise that number without interfering very much with the domestic services of the country, the Government should give warning of any intended change so that there will be no misunderstanding.

I am very much surprised to hear that the Government made any such promise as that which was first given. I think they must have become a little bit hysterical or excited at that time. The arrangement which the minister states came into effect on November 1, is absolutely fair and just. The men who joined the forces were prepared to sacri- '
fice their lives. I do not agree with my hon. friend that men who have not been sent out of the country are not just as loyal as any who have gone. They have enlisted, they have put themselves in a position to go, and they may be sent away at any moment. If they are not sent abroad it is probably not their fault. We have never seen any indication that they were not willing to go when the word was given. Simply because there are some still remaining in Canada, I would not deduct from them what they would be entitled to receive if they went to the front. If these men joined under a certain understanding or promise I do not see how the Government can honourably go back on that promise any more than an individual could. I know personally an individual wiho promised his men who joined that their salaries would be paid, and who issues his cheque every month to the men who went with that understanding. Personally, if I induced men to go to the war, or to enlist, upon a certain understanding; I would carry out that understanding as long as I was capable of doing so. I am not blaming the Government for doing what I would do personally, but at the same time I confess to the belief that the Government were carried away by excitement wh&i they made the first promise. If the men go because of their loyalty to the country it was absolutely unnecessary to make such a promise. You cannot get away from anomalies in the trenches any more than you can in private or commercial life. I think the arrangement beginning on the first of November last is perfectly right and proper. I am sorry I cannot advocate the cancellation of the first arrangement, because the men joined on the understanding that it would be carried out.	-

Do I understand from the Prime Minister that the arrangement was made that the Government would pay all men who enlisted their full salaries for the duration of the war? The Government has the precedent established by railway and other corporations which undertook to pay their men for six months or a year.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
That may be the case with some corporations, but I know there are other corporations who are paying their men at the front, and propose to pay them during the whole period of the war their full salaries while they are absent, and to keep their places open for them. Doubtless if the Government had anticipated that the war would continue so

long we might have made, in the first instance, the arrangement that was made on the first of November last. But, in the course which we did pursue, we were only adopting the same policy as that which was adopted by many private individuals and public corporations throughout the country.

This is a very large amount of money-nearly half a million dollars. I would like to know how this amount stands as compared with the amount for the same services during previous years. I see that this is the same amount as was voted last year. How far back does it run at the same amount, or has there been in recent years, an increase or a decrease? There are certain questions I would like to ask, and I might ask them collectively, so that they could be answered after eight o'clock if desirable.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: We have the Estimates here for last year and this year, but I have nothing here that goes back further than that. I could give the information to the hon. gentleman at a later sitting.

I would like to know what the yearly amount for this service has been for, say, the past five years. Then I would like to know what has been the amount of the services rendered or called upon in each of the same years in the matter of homestead entries, homestead patents, and the collection of moneys in payments on pre-emptions and purchased homesteads.

In view of the need for economy during the war, would it not be possible for the minister to reduce this item? When I was out West a few months ago, I ran across an outside service official, a timber ranger for the Department of the Interior in the district north of Winnipeg. This man was dismissed two or three years ago on the ground that his services were no longer required. He told me that when working for the department he received a Salary during only certain months of the year and a certain amount for expenses. Three men had since been engaged, he said, to do the very work that he had done himself, and they were each drawing $100 or $125. a month all the year round, and expenses. Now, if one man can do that work, and will do it for a much less salary, it seems to me that the minister could practise economy in that very case. I notice that the reduction this year amounts to only a few million dollars in an expendi-

ture of $150,000,000, to $160,000,000. The
percentage of reduction is very small, and I think the minister could help out the Minister of Finance by reducing this particular item. I do not know of any other item in the whole Estimates that could be cut down with less injury to the public service. I might tell my hon. friend that his predecessor the present Minister of Public Works took on a great number of unnecessary men, and I would suggest that the minister let some of these men out; he could do it without injury to the public service, whatever harm it might do to the ex-minister. I venture to say that this item could be reduced by $100,000 without the public service suffering in the slightest degree.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: The hon. member will agree that the word of a dismissed official is not always the most reliable or impartial; but if it is true that three men are now engaged where there was only one official heretofore, I think I can suggest a reasonable explanation. The hon. gentleman knows that a certain section of the country has been filling up very rapidly during the last three or four years. A large number of homestead entries have been made between Lake Manitoba and Lake Winnipeg, which [DOT] of course makes more work for our officials. I might also say that last year our whole outside staff-range inspectors, homestead inspectors, and other officials-turned in and assisted in the seed grain work, on which we spent $13,000,000 last year. More than that, we had to engage extra help, temporarily, to assist., in the work. I think it would be false economy to reduce our staff as the hon. member suggests, for in the event of a similar emergency occurring this season we would simply have to engage outside help again. The Estimates for the Department of the Interior' this year are $1,800,000 less than last year's estimates.

Was the whole of last
year's vote expended?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: All except $7,000 or $8,000.

The Finance Minister
told us this afternoon that we should economize, that we should cut out luxuries and buy essentials only. He called attention to the fact that he expected to spend only $135,000,000 next year. Now, these Estimates call for an expenditure of $158,000,000. Therefore, $23,000,000 has to be cut out by somebody, and I think the Interior Depart-

ment might lend the Finance Minister a hand in this particular item. There are, I think, fifteen departments of the Government altogether; that would mean that each department should cut down its Estimates by $1,500,000.	'

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: My reduction is over

My hon. friend has done pretty well on the total, but I think on this particular item he could make a nice reduction and spend the money, if he must spend it, on something that is more urgently needed. There is another point. Are we to understand that officials of the Department of the Interior who have enlisted reecive their full salary from the Government, and that the war appropriation fund makes up the difference?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Only those who enlisted before the 1st of November, 1915, are drawing civil as well as military pay. I might point out that we do not pay the substitutes as much as the permanent men. For instance, the substitute of an official drawing a salary of $1,500 would receive only about $1,200 from the war vote.

Then the department is not out anything at all; it is the war vote that is touched, not the department. Under the circumstances, therefore, I think the minister could reduce this vote by the salaries of the men who have gone off the pay-roll.
At six o'clock, the House resumed, and then took recess.
The House resumed at eight o'clock.

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext:
The House in Committee of Supply, Mr. Rhodes in the Chair.
Dominion lands and parks-contingencies, advertising, etc., $300,000.

speakerposition: subtopic
speechtext:
["As we have done a
pretty good day's work I would suggest that we adjourn.
Progress reported.
On motion of Hon. Mr. Rogers the House adjourned at 11.10 p.m.
Wednesday, February 16, 1916."]

Will the minister say
what kind of advertising this is?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: This item covers advertising re sale of timber berths, insertion of homestead and coal mining regulations, notices in connection with lands open for entry, etc.

I remember when my
hon. friend was sitting on this side of the House, not himself but some of the members of his party, notably my good and genial friend the member for Peel
(Mr. Blain), used to argue very strongly, in sitting after sitting, that even in the case of advertising, tenders should be invited. Has my hon. friend taken a leaf out of the book of the hon. member [DOT] for Peel by deciding to ask for tenders from the different papers, or does he give this advertising to the party press?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
The homestead and
mining regulations are published in the press of the country at the King's Printer's price. No tenders are asked for, but there is a standard price.

I venture to say
that the publishing of the homestead regulations is done only by a certain class of papers. My hon. friend will look in vain through the pages of the Regina Leader, the Saskatoon Phoenix and the Moosejaw Times for the homestead regulations; but he will find them in the Regina Province, the Moosejaw News, the Saskatoon Star, and other mino'r Conservative papers in the province of Saskatchewan. It is a matter of business that the homestead regulations should be published by the papers having the largest circulation in the province, or outside of it, for that matter. I suppose the minister would not care whether the coming of an immigrant into Canada was the result of an advertisement in the Saskatoon Star rather than in the Saskatoon Phoenix; I think he would be perfectly satisfied if a man came into this country as the result of the circulation of a Liberal newspaper. There must be a patronage list of some kind with respect to these newspapers.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: That would be a crime, I suppose.

When I sat on the Government side of the House I used to hear criticisms from many hon. gentlemen who are new supporting uie present Administration with respect to advertising only in certain classes of newspapers. I do not know whether I would find fault with my hon. friend if he wanted to favour his friends with some special advertising, but in a matter of this kind, which affects the whole people of the country, he should put his patronage list aside.

Has the hon. member
for Peel asked the minister to call for tenders in connection with these advertisements? [DOT]	.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
I do not recollect that at
the moment.

What are the principal
headings under which this large sum of $300,000 for contingencies, advertising, etc., is to be disbursed?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Expenses of homestead inspectors, including purchase of travelling outfits, $65,000; expenses of timber inspectors, including purchase of travelling outfits, $20,000; expenses of inspectors of ranches, $10,000; expenses of 27 Dominion lands and crown timber agencies, $60,000; travelling expenses of outside service officials when away on Government business, $35,000; items for printing and stationery, timber berths, and unforeseen expenses.
Could the minister give me any information offhand as to the number of homestead inspectors there are in Saskatchewan at the present time?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: There are 30 in Saskatchewan; 63 altogether.
Is it not correct that there has been a substantial increase in the number of homestead inspectors? *

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Yes.

I am at a loss to understand why so many homestead inspectors should be needed to-day, and why there should be so marked an increase in the number of homestead inspectors since 1911. It cannot be on account of an increase in the number of homesteads which require to be inspected. In one place with which I am familiar there are, or were for a time, four homestead inspectors, and there are scarcely any homesteads in the district. I remember the case of a homestead inspector who came to the Regina land office from the city of Moosejaw. According to information furnished to the House a year or two ago by the Minister of the Interior, this man drew his salary for four or five months, although during that period he did not inspect one solitary homestead. He had a team of horses eating their heads off in a livery stable in the town of Rouleau; during that period the horses were not used except on the occasion of a provincial election in Saskatchewan in 1912. Apparently the department did not know whether to pay this man his salary or not; but as the result of a meeting that took place at Regina between a former inspector of Dominion land agencies at Regina and three or four members of the Conservative patronage committee in that city, it was finally decided to pay the inspector his salary. This gentleman, therefore, drew

about $500 for a period of five months during which he made no inspections. If this matter had come to the attention of the minister, I have no doubt that he would not have allowed it to take the course which it did. The minister was in Regina in 1912 with the present Minister of Public Works (Mr. Rogers), then Minister of the Interior, when, with a great flare of trumpets, a large meeting was held in that city, and all sorts of promises were made to the people, which have not been fulfilled to this day. If the minister had prolonged his stay he w'ould have seen what this homestead inspector and his team did in that Saskatchewan election.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: There has, of course, been an increase in the number of homestead inspectors during the last few yeaTS. As the hon. gentleipan knows, the immigration to Canada subsequent to 1911 was the largest that we ever had. In the year ended March 31, 1913, the immigration to Canada reached the high-water mark, 412,000. In 1914 it fell off about 17,000 to about 385,000. A great many of these new immigrants settled upon the land back a considerable distance from transportation; the Peace river country has been opened up and this necessitated moTe officials. These men after being in the country for three years required inspections when they were applying for patents, and, a;S the hon. gentleman knows, the principal immigration has taken place in the northern, in the Peace river country. The larger number of homestead inspectors were appointed in northern Alberta, although there were some additional, ones in Saskatchewan. While I do not know' anything about the particular instance brought forward by the hon. member for Regina (Mr. Martin), I can quite understand a homestead inspector sometimes not being engaged in homestead inspection; frequently they are deputed to perform other duties than homestead inspection. Then, again, we often find it more convenient for homesteaders settled at considerable distances from sub-agencies to have inspectors visit them in order to obviate the necessity of homesteaders travelling great distances to make applications for patents. Certain homestead inspectors have been deputed to visit farmers practically five times.
That was done before.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
Not to the same extent. There is now, in fact, a special homestead

inspector who has been deputed during the laist few years to do this in Saskatchewan and to do nothing else. We have adopted the same principle in Alberta. I will investigate the case mentioned by my hon. friend if he will give me the name of the homestead inspector.
I

The minister pointed out that because there was an increased immigration during 1912-13 there was an increase in the number of homestead inspectors. Will he apply the same principle and, because during 1913, 1914 and 1915 there was a *decrease in the number of immigrants, decrease the number of homestead inspectors? Then in southern and central Manitoba and the eastern portions of Saskatchewan that are well settled, and where 95 per cent of the homesteads have been patented, has the number of homestead inspectors been reduced? I know that in my own part of the country, there has not been any reduction in the number, although in the greater part of that country practically all homestead lands have been patented. In connection with the Estevan land office, where Mr. Morrison is the agent, there is practically no homestead inspection to he done. Fully nine-tenths of the inspector's time is devoted to political work; he is canvassing practically all the time. I do not know that he is neglecting his duties, because I do not think there are any duties for him to perform. In the last year or two the land district was divided and a new district formed in Weyburn. It was the practice in the past for the homestead inspector to reside at headquarters, at the town where the land office was. This homestead inspector does not do that. He has been in office since the change of Government four years ago, and still lives in his old home, probably seventy-five miles or so away. He goes home over the week ends, and spends probably half his time either travelling to or from his home or at his home. Again I cannot say he is neglecting his duty, because I do not think there is any work for him to do. I know that in the newer sections of the country there is extra work, but in the settled portions of the West the decrease in the amount of inspection work to be done is quite as great as the increase in the newer sections, so that the total work of inspection could be done just as efficiently without any increase in the number of inspectors. Yet new inspectors are being constantly appointed, and there.are no reductions in the staff in the sections where there has been a falling off in the work to be done. In these sections where the homestead land has all been patented a number of inspectors could be dispensed with without any impairment of the public service.

I should like a further explanation from the minister as to the proceedings at the recent conference between the minister and the premiers of the western provinces and the Canadian Government immigration agents at Chicago. My reason for asking about this is that various reports have been published in the newspapers. I am sorry that the fire destroyed some of my papers, including clippings to the effect that the minister had given assurance, which was made public purposely, to the effect that there would be no conscription in Canada-that no matter what course the British Government took, the Government of Canada would not be guided by it. Since the fire I have looked up the Ottawa Citizen of January 31, and, while the report is very much modified from what appeared in the western papers, even there the idea is given. The despatch is as follows: Chicago, January 30.-Canada governs itself and is not influenced by Great Britain in any way; conscription never will he adopted in the Dominion, and there are no war taxes on Canadian land and never will he. These are some of the assertions here Saturday hy Dr. Wm. J. Roche, Minister of the Interior of Canada, and T. Crawford Norris, Premier of Manitoba, at the meeting of Canadian immigration agents in United States.
I asked the minister a question the other day as to the terms of tiny statement he made, and the minister's reply was as follows:
In addressing a conference of our United States immigration agents recently in Chicago for the purpose of reviewing the immigration situation and making plans for the future, the Minister of the Interior took an opportunity of making a statement refuting the false impression which had been created hy articles which have appeared in certain United States papers regarding conscription.
The answer given by the minister does not touch itbe point that has been published in the western papers, that is, as to any assurance that may have been given to the American public and to intending immigrants that there would be no conscription in Canada. I am bringing this to the attention of the House to give the minister an opportunity of making further explanation, and also for the purpose of expressing the view, which I hold very strongly, witn regard to representations made to those who may purpose coming to Canada. We are at this time at war; the Parliament of

Canada has not made any declaration in favour of conscription and is not likely to; I notice, however, that every man who has a son at the front is in favour of some form of universal service at this time.
I think all the members of this House take the position which I take, that, if necessary in the defence of this country, and for the purpose of winning this war, we should have conscription or anything else required to bring about that end. I have no doubt that the question has been raised in the United States as to whether *there will be conscription in Canada, and it is not at all improbable that immigration .agents may have asked from their minister some assurance on that point. It is not at all improbable also that some expressions of opinion may have been given. We find that many immigrants who went to the United States were born in Germany. They left Germany and went to the ' United States to escape military service; but when they got there they found they were in a country where conscription is the law of the land, because in the American Civil War conscription prevailed, great numbers of Northern troops having been raised in that way. I want to make my own attitude clear, and I want to give the minister an opportunity to state his own position, and to affirm that it would be most unwise that anything should be said in public which would lead those who live in a country where there is compulsory military service to believe that they might come into a country which is now at war and not be subject to like service. I believe that such dispatches as have been sent out misrepresent the opinion of this country, and possibly misrepresent the minister, if they have led anybody to believe that such is the policy of Canada in regard to that question.
One of my reasons for bringing up this matter is that on a previous occasion some representations wrere made to intending settlers which to-day are a source of considerable trouble. The Minister of the Interior is aware that at the present time the province of Manitoba is considering the whole question of teaching of languages other than English in the schools of the province. It appears that in what is known as. the Mennonite reserve, in the southern portion of Manitoba, the Mennonites have been accustomed to conduct private schools in which German only is taught, and which are non-English schools. I have here a letter which was published in one of the Manitoba newspapers of recent date, and

which was written by P. M. Lowe, secretary of the Department of Agriculture, on 23rd July, 1873. It was addressed to representatives of the Mennonite community who were visiting this country, and whose homes were in Russia. One of the assurances given by Mr. Lowe is contained in paragraph 1 of this letter:
An entire exemption from any military service is, by law and Order in Council, granted to the denomination of Christians called " Mennonites."
I think that was a proper thing for Mr. Lowe to say, because under our Militia Act there is an exemption in respect to bearing arms, or to military service, under prescribed conditions. But the dangerous point in Mr. Lowe's letter was with regard to the educational question. I am only quoting this letter now for the purpose of showing how dangerous it is for any person on behalf of this country to make representations upon which any settler may come to this country, and which may become a bill of rights. Here is the clause to which I refer-clause 10:
The fullest privilege of exercising their religious principles Is by law afforded to the Mennonites, without any kind of molestation or restriction whatever, and the same privilege extends to the education of their children in schools.
In the province of Saskatchewan we have, under the Mennonite Church, non-English private schools which teach only the German language. This letter was handed to me as establishing the right of the Mennonites to do so, they having been promised on behalf of the Government of Canada, before they came to this country, that they would be able to exercise their religion and to have the schools to which they had been accustomed in Russia. I am quoting it merely to show how easy it is for some persons in the Government service, no doubt well intentioned, to make a mistake which might be the cause of misunderstandings long after the members of this House had ceased to have any say in public affairs.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
I have no objection whatever to give the hon. member the information he desires in regard to what took place in Chicago, although I trust that at this stage it will not result in precipitating a debate on the question if immigration. It would be scarcely apropos in considering an item of contingencies for Dominion lands and parks to Have a discussion with regard to a department, the estimates of which

are not up for discussion to-night. However, out of courtesy to the hon. member, I have no objection to explain the position I took while attending the conference of Dominion immigration agents in Chicago. I do not know whether or not the hon. member was in the House yesterday when the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Turriff) read a somewhat similar article, if not the same article, from one of the Canadian papers regarding what I was reported to have stated, and what Premier Norris was reported to have stated in connection with conscription. But upon that occasion I informed the hon. member for Assiniboia that there were no newspaper reporters present at our conference. They are a very enterprising lot of gentlemen, and what they may have surmised I do not know, nor am I responsible. I gave no interview to any newspaper reporter while in the city of Chicago. Who gave out the information of course I do not know, but what I am responsible for is the letter in regard to conscription that has been circulated through some thousands of United States newspapers in order to correct the eroneous impression that had been scattered broadcast for the purpose of preventing immigrants from going from the United States into Western Canada. I felt it was my duty, over my own signature as Minister of the Interior, to dissipate the erroneous impression that our agents had to contend with in their propaganda for securing immigrants. What I stated was assuredly nothing more than what was stated in this House at the instance of the right hon. leader of the Opposition in the debate on the Address. The right hon. the leader of the Opposition pressed the Prime Minister to state once more his position in regard to conscription, and the Prime Minister did state that we have no conscription in Canada, and that we did not propose to have it. That is the effect of the letter which I caused to be circulated in the United States press. It was dated 8th January, 1916, and reads as follows:
Through either lack of knowledge or from some ulterior motive numerous papers in the United States have recently advised American citizens that by going to Canada they incurred the risk of being drafted as soldiers in the present world-wide war. Were these articles confined only to that portion of the pro-German press, which without regard to the truth, have been publishing fictitious news Items intended to injure the trade or stir up friction between the States and Canada, the reports might safely be let go uncontradicted, but when responsible journals are misled into publishing erroneous
information regarding conscription it seems advisable to make an official pronouncement upon the matter.
I therefore beg to advise you that all troops from Canada for the war have gone voluntarily ; that while the Government has the power to enforce conscription, such action has not been considered either advisable or necessary, and that even were conscription introduced it would apply to Canadian citizens only.	.
For your information when dealing with this subject, I may say that many Canadians resident in the United States and many American citizens have crossed into Canada since the outbreak of war, have offered their services, been acoepted, did valuable work and in some cases gave up their life in the cause of liberty and justice.	,
Any publicity you may care to give to this letter will be appreciated by,
Tours faithfully,
W. J. Roche, Minister of the Interior.
I do not think even the hon. gentleman will take exception to the statements contained in that letter, and it was precisely those sentiments that I expressed^ to our own agents there when they were telling me of the obstacles they had to encounter in securing immigrants for Canada. I realized the difficulties the hon. gentleman has spoken of, but at the same time I thought it my duty to correct the absurd rumours that had been designedly circulated in the United States for the purpose of keeping immigrants, from Canada, and which were being taken advantage of by the railways, by land companies, banks, and everybody else interested in preventing immigration to this country.
Mr. OLfVER: I do not think anybody would take exception to the letter my hon. friend has just read, and if it had received the same measure of publicity that the alleged interview received there would be no reason for discussing this matter in the House. Unfortunately, while the alleged interview was given very wide publicity, the letter has not been given anything like the same measure of publicity. Now, the difference between the position of the Premier and the leader of the Opposition, and the position of the minister, supposing the interview had been correct, is this: The Premier and the leader of the Opposition were stating the policy, one of the Government, and the other of his party, at that time. Necessarily, what is the policy of a Government, or of a party, to-day may not be the policy to-morrow, and therefore the statements made by the Premier and the leader of the Opposition were not binding upon the country for the future. But a

statement made by a member of the Government to private individuals in another country who would be prejudiced by that statement is in quite a different category. The one is in the nature of a private contract, the other is in the nature of a declaration of public policy-two different matters altogether. While, therefore, I take no- exception to the letter my hon. friend has read, and which no doubt has been duly distributed, I take the liberty of saying that in view of the very wide publicity that was given to the alleged interview, and the construction that must necessarily have been placed upon it, my hon. friend would have been well advised to have taken an early opportunity in this House of properly expressing his position and that of the Government in regard to this important matter. Of course, it is an easy way out of it to let it go, but it is not the right way, it is not the best way, and it is a way that is liable to produce unfortunate results in the future. The credit of this country at the present time, and for the future, is in a large measure in the hands of my hon. frierid, and since the misrepresentation of the facts of the case has been given wide publicity, I take the liberty of saying that it is his business, at all risks and at all costs, to see that that misrepresentation is publicly and efficiently corrected.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: I might point out that while probably tpore publicity has been given in the Canadian press to the remarks that were attributed to me than to the denial, it is quite the contrary in the press of the United States. The letter I have just read has been inserted in thousands of journals in the United States, and that is where we wish to have the facts of the case known. As for the publicity given to the alleged interview, I do not suppose that any words of mine spoken in the city of Chicago would be of sufficient importance to the people of the United States to be printed in thousands of their papers. After all, what statement contained in the alleged interview is the hon. gentleman taking exception to? Is it the statement that it is not the intention of the Canadian Govern-men to enforce conscription?

My hon. friend was in Chicago as the representative of Canada, and he is represented as assuming to have given the people of the United States a statement as to the future policy of the Government of Canada. Now, he was not

entitled to do that; it was not proper that he should do it; and as he had been represented as having done it he should have corrected the impression promptly and with all publicity. My hon. friend has said that he has done so, and of course we must accept his statement to that effect. While it is of course desirable that the correction should be made in the United States, it is also desirable that there should be a thorough understanding in Canada as to how far the Government was committed to a certain policy in connection with this country. There is another side to the question, namely, that if the Government of Canada is to be understood as making a declaration that under no circumstances will we put forth the whole strength of our people in support of our cause in this war, Canada, in. the mind of her Allies, will be put in a position that is certainly unfortunate, undesirable, and one that does not tend to success. If we are understood throughout the allied world not to be willing to do everything we can for the cause, not willing to support it to our last man and our last dollar, then we aTe weak where we should be strong, and we are doing ourselves an injury the extent of which cannot very well be estimated.

I used that argument because- the hon. gentleman said that the work had fallen off. I said that sue staff was more busily engaged last year than ever before. The minister will remember that last year there was brought to his attention the matter of the conduct of one R. H. Keay, who lived near the Riding Mountain forest reserve. As the result of an investigation held last year by an inspector sent out for that purpose, it was shown that seventeen different men in that district got homesteads by agreeing to vote Conservative. A further condition of the agreement was that each of the parties was to pay R. H. Keay the sum of $100; accordingly, each gave Keay a promissory note

for that amount. When the matter was up last year the minister stated that Keay had interviewed him, and had been severely reprimanded for his conduct. The minister also said that he would notify these men not to pay the notes-I have not Hansard here, but the impression given was that the men who had signed these notes would be protected in some way. It might be quite impossible for the minister absolutely to protect these men, but they had gathered the impression that the minister was going to protect them and that they would not have to pay the notes. speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: The hon., member has not stated the position quite accurately. It is true that he brought up this matter in the House last session, and that I explained to him that a man named R,. H. Keay, not in the employ of the Government at all, according to, his own statement to me, charged certain Galicians for marking the limits of their homesteads, certain sums of money. He took notes from a number of these people for $100 apiece. When I learned of this I instructed our inspectors to inform these men who had given notes not to pay them, that they were not liable, in my opinion, as I believed that this man had imposed upon them. I said nothing about protecting them in any way further than that. I have learned that Keay has discounted these notes in the bank, and that action has been taken against a number of the makers of the notes and judgment recorded against them. The whole matter, as I informed the hon. gentleman, has been referred by myself to the Justice Department. Although I do not think that we are legally bound to prosecute Keay, the Justice Department are taking criminal proceedings against him.

The facts are that this man Keay was a justice of the peace of the province of Manitoba at Asessippi, a village not far from Roblin. A justice of the peace, by reason of his position, is able
to exercise a great influence over these foreigners, who think thaf a man in that position has a great influence in the community. Why in the world such a man was allowed by the Dominion lands agents to use his position as a justice of the peace to impose upon these people is something I am unable to understand. There is surely something wrong with the administration of the Crown lands in that part of the country when a Tory heeler occupying the position of justice of the peace under the late Roblin Government was allowed to impose on people in that way.
Would the minister explain the duties of fire rangers in connection with timber reserves?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
Their duties are, in the

Some of these officials do not carry out their duties very well. I do not think they live in the houses built for them. There is not much danger of fire in the winter, and the rangers are required only for a few months in the fall. We have been advised by the Minister of Finance to economize. I think the Minister of the Interior could dispense with many of these fire rangers, at least until the termination of the war. There is not much lumbering going on in the West at this time, and I am quite sure that this economy could be effected without detriment to the public service.
