speechtext:
It would appear from the minister's explanation that the forest reserves have been increased for the purpose of finding employment for a large number of fire rangers. It was one of those fire rangers who told me that to do the work which he formerly did three men were now employed all the year round. The minister pointed out, and I must agree with him to a certain extent, that a dismissed official is probably not the best source of information. But according to the minister's explanation there are a number of extra fire rangers employed. I know some parts of the country where these positions are simply political appointments. While the timber reserves have been very largely increased, everybody who knows anything at all about timber in those

western reserves knows that there is bound to be a large percentage of them that have no commercial timber. The timber may grow up some time to be of some value in holding the snow and preserving the moisture, but, as I understand it, these reserves, especially the new reserves, are away from settlement to a very large extent. The payment of $100 a month to 275 fire rangers is a tremendous expenditure for the benefit we get from it, and it seems to me that if the Government wish to carry out the programme of economy laid down by the Minister of Finance this afternoon, they will have to go more steadily about it.

How many file guards have been ploughed during the last season?
I understand it is the policy of the Government to plough fire guards around the timber reserves, and I would like to know if the scheme has been successful.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: In the different reserves there was a mileage of 252, and the total expenditure was $2,614.

How much was spent in
the Riding Mountain reserve?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: I have not the figures subdivided.

There is one remark to be made in regard to this vote as in regard to the others, and that is, that notwithstanding the professed economy on the part of the Prime Minister, the Department of the Interior has not reduced its expenditure in connection with these services to meet the stringent financial conditions that have arisen from the war. It is another case of "Do as I say, not as I do."
Mr. 'CRUISE: It is very important to the settlers in the western country that these timber reserves should be protected. I have discussed with several of the leading men in the northern district the question of how best to go about it, and we have come to the conclusion that instead of ploughed fire guards there should be some co-operation between the Provincial Government, the Dominion Government, and the municipalities, in the direction of building highways between the settlements and the reserves. These highways would act as fire guards in the sense that when a fire occurred the settlers would be enabled to get to the scene of the fire more rapidly. In the Riding Mountain reserve at present if a fire starts there are no good roads to enable the settlers and fire rangers to get to it. I do not think that the Dominion Gavernment alone should pay for the highways, but they might join with the Provincial Government and the municipalities in building them round the reserves. I am certain that they would be of great benefit in the way of protecting the reserves. I think this matter was brought to the ministers's attention before by my opponent, Mr. Campbell.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
I do not recollect having
this matter brought to my attention before, but I see the force of the hon. gentleman's remarks. Of course, the building of highways does not come within the jurisdiction of the Dominion Government, but I recognize that the question of co-operation between the Provincial Governments and the Dominion Government is well worthy of consideration. I will take the suggestion into consideration, and see what steps can be taken to meet the hon. gentleman's wishes.
Dominion lands and parks-protection of reindeer herds, $3,000.
Where is the reindeer herd now?'

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
I am afraid the reindeer
herd is practically non est. I am instructed that the number has been reduced to a solitary one. The experiment has been a failure right from the start. I would remind hon. members that it was not started under my jurisdiction, but before I became minister. We have one reindeer there now, and we aTe taking good care of it, but we do not expect a renewal of this vote.
Would it not be well to cut it out this year?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: We may not expend the money this year.
Could we not persuade the minister to drop this item?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: It is very small.
It would be an evidence of good faith in reduction of the Estimates.

It would be better to bring that reindeer down and board it at the Chateau Laurier.
To pay expenses connected with water-power investigations and reports in Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta, and the Railway Belt in British Columbia, $164,000.
I would ask the minister to give us some idea of what was done last year and how much was expended.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: I have a statement of the work that we propose to spend this money-on during the ensuing year, and I find there is a reduction of $30,000 in the Estimates. It is to be expended under the following heads:	British Columbia hydrographic survey, Manitoba hydrographies survey, international waters, storage in the Winnipeg river basin, power surveys, reports, etc., in Manitoba; power surveys, reports, etc., in Alberta and Saskatchewan; storage in Saskatchewan basin, administration of small water-powers, inspection of construction, drainage and reclamation, consulting engineers, head office and administration expenses, publication of reports, special engineering report oh the water-power administration in the railway belt of British Columbia; hydrographic survey work, northern British Columbia, along the Grand Trunk Pacific in the Peace river block and Yukon territory; co-operation with the Nova Scotia Water-Power Commission. This was all spent, except a few hundred dollars, last year, and a good deal of this same work will be continued during the ensuing year.

There is no doubt that the work is very important. I am not finding fault with the investigation of water-powers which can be utilized commercially as long as the money is well expended, but it seems, to me a very large amount, although somewhat smaller than last year.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: There is no new work.

I would be inclined to go a little further than my hon. friend from Assiniboia. >
While this work is entirely desirable under favourable conditions, it is a work of investigation, upon the result of which will be based investment in the development of water powers at a later date. At the present time, and under existing financial conditions, there is no pressure of demand for the opportunity of investing money in the development of water-powers. Therefore there is no pressure for this expenditure at the present time. It is certainly one amount in the Estimates that could be very greatly curtailed this year without the public suffering any damage whatever. That is not finding any fault with the purpose of the vote or with the work that has been done. But it is not at the moment opportune or pressing, and if there is any desire on the part of this department to economize, it should be shown by the cutting down of this particular vote.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
I have given instructions to the officers preparing the Estimates to do the work with regard to the strictest economy. I have a memorandum prepared by the head of the Water-Powers Branch, in which he says that if there is any further reduction of the Estimates, it will simply paralyse their work. He says:
In response to the Deputy Minister's instructions respecting- the reductions in the Estimates ... I beg to state that... I would recommend under all the circumstances, a further reduction of $15,000 be made. This will make a total reduction of $30,000 from our Estimates for the last fiscal year, a little over one-sixth. If any further reduction is made it will simply paralyse our work. It should be stated that the Estimates, as submitted on the 18th September last, $179,000 represented a reduction of $15,000 of last year's Estimates and covered work that we considered to be absolutely essential in the best interests of our water-power administration. There were many important matters which we were exceedingly anxious to provide for, but which we considered might reasonably be postponed until after the war. It should further be pointed out that we have at the present time 16 members with the Canadian Expeditionary Forces, their salaries representing a total annual expenditure of $20,650, which is, of course, a first charge on our Estimates. The further reduction of $15,000 recommended herein makes our Estimates for this year $164,000, which total amount should be distributed in the proper proportion among the seventeen items, about which detailed information was furnished you on September 18 last.
There are no new works to be engaged upon during the coming year, or provided for in these Estimates.
To what extent is there a prospect of the reasonably early development of any one of the water powers which have been under investigation by the department during the past year?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
A great deal of the work that has been carried on in the past year has been on the Winnipeg river. Power is being developed there very extensively. The Provincial Government of Manitoba has asked us not to alienate any further water powers without their consent. They desire to make use of these powers; they have appointed a public utility commissioner with jurisdiction over such matters. We have been acting in co-operation with the commissioner there, and everything that has been done by the department has received his sanction and support. The Winnipeg river is a river on which there are enormous possibilities with regard to development of power, and some of the existing companies are applying for permission to further increase their water-

powers. Applications are now before the department for other power rights on the same river, but we have not dealt with them pending full information as to the results of these investigations.
What is the policy of the Government in dealing with these water-powers? Is it to dispose of them to private corporations, or to hold them for the people?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: As I have just intimated, the Provincial Government of Manitoba has asked us not to alienate any further water-powers without the consent of that Government. There is an application before the department now from a corporation, or from individuals, and it has received the consent and endorsement of the Provincial Government of Manitoba.
Will the same policy be adopted in the other provinces?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: We have not had any similar requests from the other provinces.
If you have no requests, do the Government not consider that these water powers should be kept for the public and not handed over to private corporations?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Is the hon. gentleman referring to any particular province?

No. I see that the vote
covers the four western provinces, and my question is whether, after you have investigated and developed these water-powers, you are prepared to hand them over to a private company rather than to reserve them for public purposes?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: What does the hon. gentleman mean by reserve them for public purposes?

A water-power might be
reserved as the public utility of a city or town, to be kept under public control and not handed over to a private corporation.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
Somebody has to develop
them. If a province is willing to see them developed by a legitimate corporation, we have regulations which they must conform to. Ever since this Government came into power I do not think there have been any large water-power concessions granted to any private individuals. There was one small concession granted to a company, but [DOT] outside of that I do not think there have been any.

I would like to direct the minister's attention to the question of diverting some of the waters of the Saskatchewan Tiver through the southern part of Saskatchewan. I do not know whether any money was spent on that work last year, but I understand that two or three years ago the Dominion Government had surveys made for the purpose of ascertaining whether it was feasible to divert wateT from the Saskatchewan river to some of the southern parts of the province where water is badly needed. I remember very well that in the local elections in Saskatchewan, in 1912, the people in the southern part of the province, wherever they got the idea from-and it must have been from supporters of the hon. minister-were firmly convinced that before long they would have streams of water from the Saskatchewan river running across their farms and into the towns where water was scarce.
I did not pay much attention to that promise myself, because my experience with this Government is that it is long on promises and short on fulfilment so far as my part of the country is concerned.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Who made the promise?

I do not know, but I do know that some of the minister's friends made the promise on the platform. The promise was certainly not made by Liberals. I certainly didn't make any such promise. I didn't believe tne story at all myself, but the matter was very generally discussed by the people in the southern part of Saskatchewan. I think the Government has actually spent some money on surveys, though I believe nothing has been lone during the last year or two. So far as this Government was concerned, I believe it was simply a fake election promise. I shall be glad to be informed by the minister whether anything can be done to furnish the people in that part of the country with the water which they are badly in need of. This would be a very proper work for the Government to perform.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
We can discuss this more fully on the next item, but I (have a memorandum here to the effect that sur-verys were made by the Department of the Interior in 1913-14 showing the feasibility of diverting water for the use of the cities of Moosejaw and Regina and the surrounding country. These surveys were made to enable the department to deal with a 'request from the Saskatchewan Govern-

ment for a. reservation of water from that stream to assist in the development of that region. No direct application for permission to divert and use the water has yet been made by the Saskatchewan Government, and there is no apparent necessity for any further survey work by this department.
Mr. MeCRANEY: Has the minister any information in his department in regard to some negotiations between the corporation of Prince Albert and the Dominion Government respecting water-power at Cole falls? I understand that the corporation entered into some big scheme which they were not able to carry through, and that they applied for assistance to the Dominion Government.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
In regard to that I might say that the appropriation asked for under this heading has been considerably reduced from that requested for the past fiscal year. The studies in connection with storage in the Saskatchewan river basin were instituted at the request of the city of Prince Albert in connection with the hydro-electric undertaking of that city at Cole falls on the North Saskatchewan river. The question of profitable hydroelectric development on both the North and South Saskatchewan rivers is wholly dependent on the storage possibilities which may be available throughout the watershed. At present, the low winter flow forms the decisive feature in the consideration of hydro-electric development on the rivers throughout the central
10 p.m. portion of the river basin, namely, throughout Southern and Central Alberta and Saskatchewan. The continuous demand for cheap power, which is in evidence in all the cities throughout the West, calls for every effort being put forth to meet the same. Whether this cheap power is obtainable from hydroelectric sources, is dependent upon the storage resources and possibilities of the basin. The extent of these is being determined by means of reconnaissance surveys, the continuation of which this appropriation is designed to cover.
Did the Dominion Government promise to assist in the scheme for diverting water from the South Saskatchewan river to the cities of Moosejaw and Regina?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Will the hon. member ask that question on the next item?
Has the minister knowledge of any proposed water-power on the Athabaska river? I presume that if there was any such project on hand, the department would have knowledge of it.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
I do not think there is
anything in the Estimates for work on the Athabaska river. I have no information on this subject; if there has been any correspondence on the matter, it has not been brought to my attention.
, Mr. OLIVER:	Would the minister be
good enough to make a note of my inquiry so that at, some later date when his Estimates are up I can get information as to whether there has been an application of this kind. If any such application has been made, I should be glad to be informed of it.
Dominion lands and parks-for surveys and works under the Irrigation Act, etc., including ?400 for P. Marchana as auditor of disbursements made by companies acquiring lands under the irrigation system, $200,000.

The minister is aware that irrigation districts are being formed in Alberta. One was known as the Taber Irrigation district. In order to raise sufficient money to build the ditches and provide the water, the whole district was bonded; but an obstacle was met in the school lands there. These school lands had been sold, but had not been paid for by the parties who had agreed to purchase them at sales held within the last two or three years, and the lands are still practically in the possession of the Government. This is a serious matter to that district, as it prevents the carrying out of this particular system. The money can be secured,
I understand, from the Canadian Pacific Railway Company if the company can secure a lien on all the lands, but the school lands are standing in the way. I understand the matter was brought to the attention of the minister, and that the statement was made that if the Alberta Government would pass an Order in Council this Government would introduce legislation to overcome the difficulty. I should like to know if that is true, and whether anything has been done.
Mr." ROCHE: It is quite true. Mr. MacLean, the. provincial secretary of Alberta, bad an interview with myself and the officials of the department, at which he promised to get the Provincial Government to pass .an Order in Council. We

were then to get legislation confirming it in connection with the school lands. The initial action, however, has not yet been taken by the Provincial Government.
What is the character oi the surveys under this vote, and what is theiir purpose?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: The expenses are divided as follows: Permanent office staff, Calgary, $34,150; permanent field staff, irrigation (Calgary), $27,300; permanent field staff, stream measurement, $19,200; irrigation administration, field work, $18,020; irrigation surveys, field work, $19,705; stream measurement, summer field work, $35,700; stream measurement, winter field work, $13,860; expenses head office staff, Ottawa, $10,000; publication of reports and printing, stationery, supplies, etc., $10,000; expenses istaff, Calgary, $3,500; new field equipment, instruments, transport, camp equipment, office supplies, Calgary, $5,000; incidentals, $3,565.
That, of course, gives the details of the expenditure, but what I want to get at is what purpose is being served by the work that is being done.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
As the hon. member will see, we have a reduction of $68,350 in the Estimates for the ensuing year, that is, a reduction of 25 per cent from the sum appropriated for the current year. The memorandum which I have is as follows:
The sum asked for will provide for carrying on only the work which is considered absolutely essential, including:
1.	The inspection of existing and proposed irrigation and water supply projects.
This is required by law in order to determine the feasibility of proposed projects and to ascertain whether or not licenses are utilizing, or are in a position to utilize, the water to which they are entitled by license. No further reductions can be made without abandoning this work in whole or in part.
2.	The continuation of the work of stream measurement.
The determination of the quantity of water available in the rivers and streams of the prairie provinces is the basis of all irrigation and water supply development and is absolutely essential to the proper administration of the Irrigation Act. Stream measurements must be carried on continuously for a long period of years in order to be of real value and any interruption seriously affects the value of the record. This work has been carried on systematically since 1908 and has been gradually extended as funds were made available so as to cover practically all streams in the southern part of the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan and the principal streams in the northern portion.
The Western Canada Irrigation Association as well as the International Irrigation Congress have repeatedly urged the continuance of this work uninterruptedly.
3. The completion of the classification of land in the eastern section of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company's irrigation tract near Bassano.
About one-half of this tract was classified during 1915 and it is expected that the remainder can be completed during 1916 if funds are provided.
The works for the irrigation of some 400,000 acres of land in this tract are now completed
and the system is in readiness for operation and the land is open for sale and settlement. The company is anxious to avoid the mistakes and serious misunderstandings which attended the colonization of the western section of this tract and this department is therefore inspecting and classifying as irrigable of non-iivi-gable all the land prior to its being offered for sale. In the western section this was not done with the result that this department had finally to intervene between the company and dissatisfied purchasers and to classify the land after it had been sold, thus necessitating readjustment of most of the sales-contracts ana water-agreements. The company is at present carrying on an active campaign for colonizing this' tract, which is at present waste and unproductive land, and if this department should now discontinue this work of classification, it would very seriously retard the settlement and development of the land.
4. The completion of surveys on the proposed Lethbridge northern irrigation project near Lethbridge, Alta.
In this district immediately north of Lethbridge some 100,000 acres of land can be economically irrigated by water taken from Oldman river near Macleod. This district has suffered severely from drought in past years, particularly in 1910 and 1914, when there was almost complete crop failure. The settlers have witnessed the prosperous development of the lr-rigated district of Coaldale, east of Lethbridge, and have repeatedly petitioned the Dominion Government to undertake the preliminary surveys necessary to determine the feasibility and probable cost of irrigating their own lands.
Surveys were accordingly undertaken m 1914 and carried on throughout 1915, which leave no doubt of the feasibility of irrigating these lands The work is not yet sufficiently completed to enable the settlers to form an irrigation district under the law enacted by the provincial legislation in 1915 at their request, and if the survey work is now abandoned no such distriot can at present be formed.
The Western Canada Irrigation Association, at its session at Bassano, Alberta, in Novem-. ber, 1915, passed a resolution strongly urging the' Dominion Government to complete these surveys in order that this district might be more fully developed. A similar resolution was passed urging the continuation of survey work to develop the feasibility of irrigating land south of Lethbridge and tributary to St. Mary and Milk rivers, but this work cannot be continued with the limited sum asked for m this reduced Estimate.
This practically is the explanation.

A great deal of money is being expended on irrigation surveys. I am inclined to think that the Government, in districts where there is a lack of mois-

ture, and at the same time where the soil is suitable for agriculture, might go into the establishment of these small irrigation systems. In nearly all the western states the American Government has undertaken the establishment of irrigation systems; lands have thus been reclaimed and settled, and the republic has gained by reason of that policy. In my own district there is what is known as the Iron Springs project, to supply water from the Old Man river. It was made clear to the people there that they would have to form themselves into an irrigation district like the Taber district, bond the district and practically provide the system themselves. Now there exists amongst people who have studied the question quite a strong opinion that the Government might very well go into the establishment of these systems instead of placing the responsibility upon the people or giving the privilege to private companies ; because the experience of the United States warrants us in saying that the adoption of such a system in western Canada would be beneficial to the country.
I am merely making this suggestion, and I would ask the minister whether the Government has anything in view in that direction after spending so much money on irrigation surveys. During the past year a number of survey parties were through the southern part of Alberta gathering information about the possibility of irrigating large sections of that country.
Mr. ROCHE,: We have been requested to undertake this as a Government work. A deputation which came down here from that district merely asked us to do what we are doing now with this Estimate, that is, to allow them to form a company themselves, bond the district, raise the funds, and work in co-operation; but our system as it is at present differs from that in the United States, where the Government has undertaken such work as' a Government enterprise, although it charges the people the cost just the same. We are carrying on these surveys at the expense of the public treasury; the result of them is given gratis to the farmers, and they can carry on the work under provincial legislation.
Dominion lands and parks-Canadian National Parks, $349,670.

What information can
the minister give with regard to reported mishandling of funds in connection with the administration of Jasper park during the last summer?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Charges were made against the administration of Jasper park so far as certain officials were concerned, but I do not think they involved any misappropriation of funds.

Where are the national
parks of Canada situated?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
Our national parks are
situated in western Canada. The parks in the Rocky mountains are: Jasper park, Rocky Mountains park, Waterton Lakes park, Buffalo park, Elk Island park Yoho and Glacier park, Revelstoke park.
What is the use of these parks?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
I think they are of great
utility. They attract a large number of foreign tourists and cause to be spent in Canada much money that would not otherwise come into the country. As an illustration, I may point out that during the last year some 50,000 foreign tourists visited the Rocky mountains park alone. If they spent only $100 each, that would mean that $5,000,000 was spent in Canada by those visiting this park. I think it is well worth while doing something to beautify our parks, which are one of the greatest advertisements that Canada could possibly have.

Could not some of them
be established in eastern Canada as well?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: The Dominion Government do not own the lands in eastern Canada.
I should like to obtain some information with regard to charges of misappropriation in connection with the administration of Buffalo park.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
The following memorandum was prepared in connection with tne administration of Buffalo park:
Last August Mr. Silas Carpenter, Assistant Commissioner of Dominion Police, located at Banff, was instructed to make an investigation of conditions at Buffalo park. As a result, the following officers were dismissed: W. E. D. McTaggart, superintendent; W. Terpenning, gate-keeper; W. Douglas, farmer. The evidence collected indicated that these men were Joint owners in a farm close to Buffalo park and that they used Government seed oats and Government teams and implements for its cultivation. It was also shown that they were joint owners in a herd of cattle which grazed on the Buffalo park range. There were also a number of minor Irregularities. In addition, the superintendent failed to collect the amount of an over-payment he had made to the Imperial Lumber Company in connection with the purchase of lumber. It is calculated that the over-payment amounted to about $600. Instructions have been issued for the issue of a

writ against this company for the recovery of the money. An equivalent amount of seed oats has been returned to the department, and salary cheques of those three men covering a month and eight days are still held by the department. There are a number of other po nts upon which additional information is desired, and Mr. Carpenter has been instructed to make a further investigation. Mr. A. G. Smith has been appointed as superintendent in succession to Mr. MeTaggart. Permanent appointments have not yet been made to fill the other vacancies. Mr. W. H. Walker is acting as general foreman and farmer, and Mr. W. Gano is acting as gate-keeper and rider.

Is there any item in
that memorandum connecting the names of Mr. Campbell and Mr. Hudson of Wain-wright with this nefarious scheme?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: No, nothing has come out so far indicating that either of these gentlemen has been implicated in any way. As the memorandum states, Mr. Carpenter has been instructed to conduct a further investigation.

It is my opinion that
Mr. Campbell was implicated in some indirect way in the erection of a barn in the park. However, that is mere rumour.
I trust that I may get definite information later, when the minister has the whole facts as contained in Mr. Carpenter's report.

Four or five years ago, when the late Government went out of power, provision had been madh for placing a number of buffalo on the Moose mountain timber reserve, and three or four sections were obtained for that purpose. About the time that the change of government took place, or possibly after this Government came into power, tenders were called for the fencing of this land. The Moose mountains, which are in my constituency, have come to be a popular summer resort. People come there from different parts of Manitoba, Saskatchewan, and Alberta. I was up there one Sunday last summer, and in one part of the park I saw about 220 automobiles, which had come from all parts of the surrounding country, and many of which had been driven seventy-five miles in order that the owners might spend a pleasant day at the park. It had been decided years ago to put a herd of buffalo in that park, but as the park was not fenced, and the buffalo were somewhat wild, it was feared that they might escape and cross the boundary line, which is only fifty miles to the south. The buffalo at Banff have been fenced in for many years, .and are very quiet, so that there would not be the slightest danger in bringing them down to
the Moose mountains. It is hardly necessary to say that the presence of fifty or one hundred head of buffalo would be a great drawing card for that summer resort. If the park were fenced in and even twenty-five or thirty buffalo were brought down, a very good purpose would be served. Perhaps the minister can tell how many buffalo there are in Buffalo park.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Over 2,000.

It is isdimptty 'a question, therefore, of carrying out the idea which the late Government had in view when they went out of power. I should be glad to get an assurance from the minister that during the coming summer the necessary fencing will be done, and that a number of buffalo will be brought into the Moose mountain district. When this Government came into power they sent one or two men to Buffalo park to find out something about handling buffalo, but since that time nothing has been done. Every yeaT when I am out there the people ask me what the Government are going to do, and I have never been able to give them a satisfactory answer. I hope now that the minister will put me in a position to give a satisfactory answer to the people in the vicinity of Moose mountain. Let me assure the minister it would be a great advantage to that whole southern district of Saskatchewan. Few of those people have ever seen, a wild buffalo, and it would give them a great deal of pleasure and satisfaction to have a herd established there.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
Of course, it was recognized some time ago that sooner or later the large herd at Buffalo park would, have to be broken up and distributed to other parts. It is true that a small area was purchased -with the idea of eventually removing the buffalo to the district referred to. I understand it is in a forest reserve, and that is why so many people go up there, owing to its beautiful location. The reason the Government have not thus far carried out the original project is that the land has been pronounced by the inspectors unsuitable for buffalo, as there is too much timber on it. A recommendation has been made to us to purchase some land in the Indian reserve adjoining, but I am not able to say whether these lands have been surrendered. The Indians, of course, would have to give their consent and surrender the lands. My hon. friend asks me to promise that something will be done this year. Owing to my efforts to economize, I am afraid I cannot give a

promise of that kind. Hon. members criticise me for not reducing the expenditure under this and other items; but this project would necessitate a considerably larger expenditure.

The minister is wrong
in two particulars-
Only two?

-in connection with this one item. One is that, I do not care who the inspector is, if he reports that that land is unsuitable owing to the amount of timber on it, he does not know what he ds tallbing about. I lived beside that place for many years, and the timber on it would not hurt anybody or anything. I think the difficulty was not that the land was not satisfactory, but that there was not enough of it, not more than four sections; and so it was suggested that a part of the present Indian reserve should be secured. Two Indian reserves on the west end of Moose mountain were released, the land sold and the Indians brought over to the present reserve, which is more to the east. I doubt if it would now be possible to get a release of that part of the reserve. But there is any amount of land in the vicinity that could be secured that would be satisfactory. My hon. friend speaks of economizing, but this is the first item in which he proposes any reduction. We have passed millions of dollars to-night for items in which there has been no retrenchment, and the total expense will be greater than in years gone by. If my hon, friend wishes me to practise economy I am willing to do it, and if it is from motives of economy that this park is not stocked with buffalo,
I am willing to accept that answer; but I do not see why that particular item of expenditure should be cut out altogether.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: It was not included last year.

I know that, but the Government bought that land, and called for tenders for putting up the fence. They sent their employees to Buffalo park to learn how to handle the buffalo, and they have now cut all that out. It was not cut out on account of economy; why it was cut out I do not know. My hon. friend now says it was because the land was reported on as being unsatisfactory owing to the timber on it. That is not a sufficient reason. There is a large area of open land in it, 
the land is all suitable for running domestic cattle, and any land that is suitable for running domestic cattle is suitable for buffalo. I would ask the minister, in his capacity as Superintendent General of Indian Affairs, if any attempt has been made to secure a release of the lands recommended by the inspector to be secured from the Indian reserve.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: I am not sure whether such an attempt has been made or not. The information given to me was that, after an inspection of the land, it was pronounced unsuitable for the keeping of buffalo, largely on account of there being too much timber. That may or may not be so. I have no personal knowledge of the land, and I will not make a promise to the hon. member to respond to his request by including anything in the Estimates for this purpose. I have cut down the Estimates for the Canadian National Parks for this year by $300,000, and I do not see how I could reduce it further. I do not want to add to it by including an item for the purchase of lands for something that is not pressing for the present year.

I quite agree with what the minister has said, that this is not a measure of prime importance; and war time, when we ought to be economizing, is certainly not a time to buy new lands and thus add to the expenditure. But here the land was purchased, and the excuse given is that it is not suitable. 1 am not going to press the matter, because it is a small matter after all, and I am quite willing that the Government should economize. But it looks to me as if they were economizing in this matter and were not attempting to economize in larger matters.
Will the minister give details as to the number of animals in the Wain wright, Buffalo, and Elk Island parks?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: There are 2,080 in the Buffalo park.
There are some other animals besides buffalo in the Wainwright park, are there not?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Yes, the animals in Elk Island park are: Buffalo, 108; moose, 39; elk, 50; and mule deer, 6. In Buffalo park: Buffalo, 2,080; moose, 17; elk, 57; mule deer, 100; and antelope, 3.

Is anything being done at present in regard to the sale of buffalo

meat in connection with the animals slaughtered through accident or in any other way in these parks?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
There were a few
slaughtered, and tenders were called for regarding the disposition of the meat.
These tenders did not include the hides or the heads?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: No.
What is done with these?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: The heads we have at present are being mounted; they have not been disposed of.
How many animals have been slaughtered during the past year?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Only five or six.

Do I understand that the minister agrees to the suggestion that between now and next session he will look into the matter I referred to, and see whether he can secure some additional land on Moose Mountain, or whether such land would be suitable for a small herd of buffalo, so that next year we may have some assurance that something is going to be done to carry out the intention of the Government announced a few years ago to make some use of the land that has been secured?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Exception has been taken to-night to the Government's policy respecting another matter, and I would not like to say what may be included in our Estimates next -session. But I will promise to have a re-inspection of the lands we already possess, and to get all information I possibly can on the subject.

I would like to draw the attention of the minister to some complaints I have had about the grazing lease in the Waterton Lakes park. I had considerable correspondence regarding the matter, but unfortunately it was destroyed in the fire in the Parliament buildings. I think the lease is held by -a man named West, and the complaint is that the people in the surrounding district, mostly small farmers, are unable to get any of this land for grazing purposes unless they go to him and pay toll. There is a great deal of indignation in the country surrounding the park on that account. It is also charged that the first application for this lease was not given consideration, and that the man who secured the lease was a favourite, and he prevents other people from getting
access to the grazing land except at a price fixed by him. I may be mistaken in some of the statements I have made, because I have not the correspondence, but that is my recollection of the complaints made by the settlers.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: The hon. member is incorrect in stating that any lease has been issued for any portion of the Waterton Lakes park. No leases axe issued whatever, only permits, and no exclusive privilege is given to any man. .

With regard to what the ihon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Turriff) has said as to the establishment of a small herd of buffalo at Moose mountain, I would make the suggestion that the buffalo should be scattered in different localities in case of fire attacking any particular pasture, or in case of disease getting into any particular herd. It would be a form of insurance of the herd to have them scattered in as many localities as possible. The reason why no advantage was taken of the locality of Moose mountain at the beginning was the reason given by the hon. member for Assiniboia. The situation is considered to be very suitable in every way, but at that time it was thought to be too close to the international boundary, and that there was - a possibility of losing the animals that might be herded there. It was always contemplated that there should be a portion of the herd located there. I would like to ask who is in charge of Jasper park?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: A man from the head office of the name of Johnston.
Who was in charge before him?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Mr. Harvey is acting superintendent.
There was a Mr. Maynard Rogers in charge at one time, was there not?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Yes, but he has enlisted for overseas service. He was superintendent of the park.
Who succeeded him?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Mr. Harvey is acting in his absence. There was another man of the name of Sparks, who had the general management, but under the supervision of Mr. Harvey, who was appointed by the department to act in the absence of Mr. Maynard Rogers.

speakerposition: subtopic

speechtext: Is Mr. Sparks connected with the park now?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Mr. Sparks has ibeen transferred to Wainwright park.

The case of Mr. Rogers, who, I see, has been appointed aide-de-camp to General Lessard, would come within the discussion that took place this afternoon. Does Mr. Rogers draw his salary as superintendent of the park as well as his allowance as a lieutenant-colonel?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior

speechtext: I suppose the minister does not know what the allowance of a lieutenant-colonel is?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: No.

My information is that Col. Rogers, although he volunteered at an early stage of the war, has not yet been fortunate enough to be able to give his services in the fighting line; in fact, he has been on duty in England ever since going across there. In face of that fact it seems to me that Mr. Rogers comes high.
What is the system followed in awarding these grazing leases in the park? Is it open to the public in the surrounding district to make application?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Yes.

Are they notified
publicly?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Any person in the immediate neighbourhood who desires may ascertain what the regulations are. The inspector, or the man in charge of the park, estimates as to the number of stock a given area can maintain, and then he will issue permits to any persons applying for the same to cover that area. There is no exclusive privilege given to any one man. I do not know whether they take them in accordance with their order of priority, but the superintendent of the park grants permits when applied for covering the amount *of stock he estimates the park can carry.
Is there a limit to the amount of stock a man can run under a lease?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
As much as the area will
maintain.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior

speechtext:
I imagine that under
ordinary circumstances ilt would toe possibly out of place to say anything in this connection under these estimates. But we must consider Col. Rogers as an officer of the Interior Department so long as the Interior Department is paying him $2,500 a year salary. He has been given Heave of absence with salary in consideration of the military (services that he is (able to render and that be is being called upon to render. Where the salary is as large as it is in this (case, the question of the value of Col. Rogers' military service anight very welM come up for consideration on the part of the department, from this point of view, that, if Col. Rogers is not rendering the most valuable military service, he might very well be permitted to depend) upon hais military pay. So long as he is (satisfactory to the military authorities, we have nlo fault to find with him, tout if he is not rendering valuable military 'service, it sesmis to toe a little out of the way that he should he drawing such a handsome salary from the Interior Department in consideration of the military service that he does not render. This is not a pleasant matter to speak of; but, 'as a matter of fact, Col. Rogers was placed in command of a toat-talion at Valcartier, displacing the colonel who had raised the battalion, and I am given to understand that, on his arrival in England, it was found necessary to displace

him, 'because foe -was not found to foe efficient, and itfoiait he has been in what is called the reserve (battalion ever 'since foe arrived in England. I have no criticism to offer of the military arrangements; but I do submit that an employee of the Interior Department, having in good faith, of course, offered his services, and these services not having been found to be of serious value, the Interior Department is entitled to consider whether it is warranted in giving him further leave with salary.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: I do not think I would be justified in selecting Col. Maynard Rogers and assuming from what the hon. gentleman has stated that he is not performing sufficient military service to entitle him to double pay. He has been treated exactly in the same way as every other civil servant who enlisted prior to the first of November. The general Order in Council, under which all civil servants enlisting prior to that time were allowed their civil pay, is the one governing in this case, and the pay allowed to Col. Rogers is exactly in accordance with it. I take it that as Minister of the Interior I have nothing to do with Col. Rogers' military service, be it satisfactory or unsatisfactory, and I am not going to butt into the Militia Department to find out whether it is or not. I think it would be unreasonable to ask me as Minister of the Interior to inquire whether Col. Rogers' military service is satisfactory or not and I would not consider it my duty to treat Col. Rogers in a manner different from anybody else who has gone under similar conditions. I think the hon. gentleman will realize the reasonableness of the position I take.

I do not wish to single out Col. Rogers or to make any special comment in regard to him. I have mentioned his case for the purpose of bringing to the attention of the minister the information that has been given to me-and this is not by any means an isolated case-of officials of the Government volunteering for military service and whose services have not been found to be of military, value. The minister says that this is not any of his business as head of the department. I am going to take the position of disagreeing with him on that point. I think it is the business of the different members of this Government to find out whether the service that these officers are rendering is of military value or not, and to govern their dealing with these gentlemen
with that information in hand. Certainly, if there is any considerable number of officials of this Government who ostensibly have volunteered for military service and are not now rendering military service while drawing salary from this Government, that amounts to a very serious scandal and certainly should not be allowed to continue. I am compelled, with all due respect, to disagree with the minister that it is no concern of his what military service officials of his department render when they are on leave. I think that unless they are rendering valuable service, their leave and salary should be stopped.
Dominion lands and parks-engraving, lithographing, printing, and preparation of maps, plans, and kindred publications of the Dominion, including necessary materials for same, *76,150.
I must congratulate the minister on the last atlas of the Dominion. It was an excellent piece of work.

Does this item include
immigration literature?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: No.
May I ask whether the atlases can be sent to the universities and high schools upon application to the department?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
Yes.
Dominion lands and parks-grant to Alpine Club of Canada, *1,000.

What does the Alpine
Club do?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
This club, formed some
years ago, has almost a world-wide reputation. Its membership is steadily increasing, and consists of the most prominent people in all countries of the world. This grant is to assist the club.

I understand that the
department has brought some guides from Switzerland?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Not that I am aware of.
I know that some gentlemen have been brought out from Switzerland. Perhaps they are employed by the Canadian Pacific railway.

Might I ask the minister a question abouit the internment camp at Jasper park? Is it intended to utilize the labour of the prisoners interned there, and, if so, on what conditions, and for what purpose?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
I understand that about two hundred prisoners are interned there, and t'hait they are paid twenty-five cents a day for clearing up the park, building roads, clearing away the brush, etc. There are 200 prisoners at Banff, 200 at Field, and 200 at Jasper. The railways give us a very low rate for transporting these
11 pun. men to the camps. It was thought that it would be better for the men to be doing some work rather than eating their heads off.
Does the Parks Department pay them?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Yes.
Is the labour compulsory? Under what condition is the work done?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: We have supervising officers to see that the prisoners do the work. The work is not voluntary on the part of the prisoners; they are taken there and put to work; foremen are put over them to see that the work is done properly. Of course, the prisoners will not have to do much work to earn twenty-five cents a day; but we thought that we could get a lot of work done in this way.

It strikes me as a very serious problem. These people have not committed any crime against the laws of the country, and, while I can quite appreciate the desirability of interning them and offering them the opportunity of employment, when it comes down to compulsory employment at twenty-five cents a day I am afraid that that involves principles which we cannot all subscribe to.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: In view of the manner in which the British prisoners in Germany are being treated, I do not think there will be any international complications.

Referring to an item that has been passed, I should like to call the minister's attention to the latest publication of the Conservation Commission, which contains a very remarkable report by a representative of the province of Quebec on the better protection of our forests. The report is made by Mr. Piche, who is at the head of the Forestry branch in our province. Sir Clifford Sifton and the other members of the commission frankly admitted that probably the best plan to follow as regards protection against forest fires was the system adopted in the province of Quebec. That is so well recognized that the province of New Brunswick has already

borrowed some of our officials to establish the very same system in that province. I am sure my hon. friend will be interested in reading that report. I was particularly struck myself with the unanimity with which all the interested parties declared that the province of Quebec was far ahead of all other provinces in the matter of protection against forest fires.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
Similar representations
have been made to me.

As we have done a
pretty good day's work I would suggest that we adjourn.
Progress reported.
On motion of Hon. Mr. Rogers the House adjourned at 11.10 p.m.
Wednesday, February 16, 1916.
